Design studies were performed on continuous filament wound grid-stiffened composite fuselage structures using isogrid, orthogrid, and generalized orthogrid concepts.
Donnell-type shell theory including transverse shear deformation was used to analyze buckling behavior.
The study considered three buckling modes: general instability, crippling (rib buckling), and skin buckling.
A cylindrical shell of 99 cm diameter and 116.8 cm height was used as a representative fuselage section.
AS4/3502 graphite/epoxy composite material was used for skin and stiffeners with volume fractions of 65% for isogrid and 50% for orthogrid stiffeners.
Loading cases included uniaxial axial compression of 175 kN/m (1000 lb/in) and combined axial compression with torsion.
Stiffener aspect ratios of 6, 8, and 10 were studied, with higher aspect ratios reducing weight but becoming impractical beyond 10.
Isogrid designs with (0°, 90°) skin layups and orthogrid/generalized orthogrid designs with (±45°) skin layups were found optimal for weight efficiency.
Weight savings of 20-30% compared to metal fuselage designs are achievable with these composite concepts.
The isogrid concept shows superior damage tolerance characteristics compared to orthogrid and generalized orthogrid.
The continuous filament winding process prevents fiber clustering and maintains fiber alignment along stiffener axes.
Imperfections in shells due to manufacturing are not explicitly modeled but designs maintain margins to accommodate them.
The Galerkin method was used to approximate buckling loads under combined loading.
Typical stiffener thickness is about 1.22 mm (0.048 in) with heights ranging from 3 to 6 mm depending on aspect ratio.
Skin layups studied include symmetric (0°, 90°) and (±45°) fiber orientations.
The transverse shear stiffness in ribs is largely controlled by resin matrix and filler properties.
Buckling analyses assume simply supported boundary conditions for skin and clamped fixity for ribs at nodes.
The study used micromechanics to derive effective properties of stiffeners based on filler volume content.
The design approach aims to avoid interaction between global and local buckling modes by ensuring global buckling loads are lower.
Automated manufacturing methods and co-curing of stiffeners and skin are key to producing these composite fuselage structures.
